title: Lua Scripting
subtitle: EVAL, EVALSHA, and atomic multi-command operations
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Some operations require reading a value and conditionally writing based on it — a classic read-modify-write pattern. Without atomicity, a concurrent request can change the value between your read and write, causing race conditions.
whyItExists.solution: Redis executes Lua scripts atomically. No other command runs while a script is executing. This lets you combine GET + conditional SET + INCR + EXPIRE into one atomic operation without risk of interleaving.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Atomic conditional updates (compare-and-swap), complex rate limiters, distributed lock acquire/release, deduplication logic, any multi-step operation that must be atomic.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Simple operations already covered by native Redis commands. Lua scripts block the server — keep them short and fast. Redis 7.0 Functions are the modern replacement for persistent scripts.

explainModes.beginner: Sometimes you need to do several things in a row in Redis without anyone interrupting you in the middle. Lua scripting is like asking Redis to run a little program for you, all at once, with no interruptions.
explainModes.simple: EVAL script numkeys key1 key2 arg1 arg2 runs a Lua script on Redis. The script can call Redis commands via redis.call(). It runs atomically — no other Redis command runs until the script finishes.
explainModes.standard: Redis executes Lua via the embedded LuaJIT interpreter. Scripts run in the single-threaded event loop — atomically, with no interleaving. KEYS and ARGV arrays receive keys and arguments. redis.call() runs Redis commands; redis.pcall() catches errors. EVALSHA runs a previously cached script by its SHA1 hash.
explainModes.technical: Lua scripts must declare all accessed keys in the KEYS argument for cluster compatibility — Redis uses them to determine the hash slot. Scripts run in a sandboxed environment with no network, file, or system access. Time limit: 5 seconds (lua-time-limit in redis.conf) before Redis logs a warning and starts accepting SHUTDOWN and SCRIPT KILL. SCRIPT LOAD caches a script server-side; EVALSHA uses the cached version without retransmitting the script text.
explainModes.deepDive: Redis 7.0 introduced Redis Functions (FUNCTION LOAD / FCALL) as a replacement for EVAL. Functions are named, persistent across restarts, and can have libraries. They support both Lua and future engines. Scripts loaded with EVAL are ephemeral — they're cached by SHA1 but not persisted in RDB/AOF by default. Use SCRIPT EXISTS to check if a script is cached before EVALSHA.

content.text: Consider a rate limiter: GET counter, increment it, check the limit, SET it back. Between the GET and SET, another request could increment the counter too — causing a race condition. Lua scripts execute as a single atomic unit, eliminating this problem.

content.code:
# EVAL script numkeys [key ...] [arg ...]
# KEYS[1] = 'counter:page1', ARGV[1] = '1'

EVAL "
  local val = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
  if not val then val = 0 end
  local newval = tonumber(val) + tonumber(ARGV[1])
  redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], newval)
  return newval
" 1 counter:page1 1

# Returns the new value: (integer) 1

content.text: Scripts receive two arrays: KEYS for Redis key names, and ARGV for other arguments. Always pass key names through KEYS — this is required for Redis Cluster to route correctly.
Redis 7.0 introduced Redis Functions as a named, persistent alternative to EVAL scripts. Functions survive restarts and are stored in RDB/AOF.

content.code:
# Load a named function library
FUNCTION LOAD "#!lua name=mylib\nredis.register_function('myfunc', function(keys, args) return redis.call('GET', keys[1]) end)"

# Call the function
FCALL myfunc 1 mykey

# List functions
FUNCTION LIST

# Delete a library
FUNCTION DELETE mylib

content.text: Scripts run atomically and block the entire Redis server. Keep Lua scripts short — aim for microseconds, not milliseconds. Any Lua that takes >5 seconds triggers a warning and can be killed with SCRIPT KILL.
Always declare all Redis key names in the KEYS argument. Hardcoding keys inside the script breaks Redis Cluster routing — the cluster can't determine which shard to route to.

questions.question: Why are Redis Lua scripts atomic?
options: Redis locks all keys used by the script
Redis is single-threaded and runs the script without interruption from other commands
questions.explanation: Redis's single-threaded event loop means no other commands execute while a Lua script runs. Atomicity is a consequence of single-threading, not explicit locking.

questions.question: What is the advantage of EVALSHA over EVAL?
options: EVALSHA runs the script without retransmitting its full text — only the SHA1 hash is sent
EVALSHA works in Redis Cluster; EVAL does not
questions.explanation: EVALSHA references a script previously cached with SCRIPT LOAD by its SHA1 hash, avoiding retransmission of the script text on every call. This saves bandwidth for large scripts called frequently.

questions.question: Why should key names always be passed through KEYS and not hardcoded in the script?
options: Redis Cluster uses KEYS to determine which node to route the script to
ARGV only accepts strings, not key names
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster needs to know which hash slots a script accesses to route it to the correct node. Only keys declared in the KEYS parameter are visible to the cluster router.

faq.a: EVALSHA runs a previously loaded script by its SHA1 hash, avoiding resending the script text on every call. Use SCRIPT LOAD to cache the script first.

faq.q: How do I handle errors in Lua scripts?
faq.a: Use redis.pcall() instead of redis.call() to catch errors — it returns a Lua table with an 'err' field instead of raising. redis.call() propagates errors to the caller.

faq.q: What is the time limit for Lua scripts?
faq.a: 5 seconds by default (lua-time-limit in redis.conf). After that, Redis logs a warning but lets the script continue. Use SCRIPT KILL to terminate a running script (only works if no writes have been done yet).
